content: The World Health Organization (WHO) has developed clinical and policy guidelines to address intimate partner violence and sexual violence against women. These guidelines aim to provide evidence-based recommendations for healthcare providers on how to appropriately respond to such violence, including clinical interventions and emotional support. They also seek to raise awareness among healthcare providers and policymakers about the importance of addressing violence against women and the need for a comprehensive health-sector response. The guidelines emphasize the role of healthcare providers as the first point of contact for survivors of intimate partner violence or sexual assault. Women who experience violence often seek medical care for their injuries, even if they do not disclose the associated abuse. Statistics show that abused women use healthcare services more frequently than non-abused women and often identify healthcare providers as the professionals they trust most to disclose abuse. The guidelines are based on systematic reviews of evidence related to identifying and providing clinical care for survivors of intimate partner violence, clinical care for sexual assault survivors, and training healthcare providers to address these issues. They also include policy and programmatic approaches for delivering services and address mandatory reporting of intimate partner violence. The recommendations are designed to serve as a foundation for national guidelines and to integrate these issues into healthcare provider education. They aim to improve the capacity of healthcare providers to care for women experiencing sexual assault and intimate partner violence. Although men can also be victims of partner violence and sexual assault, the guidelines focus on women because they experience higher rates of sexual violence, more severe physical violence, and greater coercive control from male partners. However, some of the advice may also be relevant for violence against women by family members other than intimate partners, partner abuse of men, and sexual assault of men. The target audience for these guidelines includes healthcare providers, as they are uniquely positioned to address the health and psychosocial needs of women who have experienced violence. The guidelines also aim to inform policymakers and those responsible for developing training curricula in medicine, nursing, and public health. Additionally, they include guidance for service delivery and program implementation for those developing, funding, and implementing programs to address violence against women. The development of these guidelines followed a rigorous process outlined in the WHO Handbook for Guideline Development. This process involved identifying clinical and policy-related questions, retrieving and synthesizing up-to-date evidence, formulating recommendations with input from a wide range of stakeholders, and planning for dissemination, implementation, and updating. The evidence supporting the recommendations was synthesized using the GRADE (Grading of Recommendations Assessment, Development, and Evaluation) methodology for clinical interventions. For policy and healthcare delivery questions, descriptive evidence was summarized, and the strengths and weaknesses of different approaches were identified. The Guideline Development Group (GDG) included academics, clinicians, service providers, policymakers, and advocates working on women’s health and violence against women, particularly in lowand middle-income countries. The recommendations were developed during a meeting at the WHO office in Geneva and considered evidence, the balance of benefits and harms, women’s preferences and human rights, and cost implications in different countries and communities. For clinical interventions, the quality of evidence was graded as very low, low, moderate, or high using the GRADE methodology. In some cases, existing guidelines were partially relied upon, and the quality of evidence in those guidelines was assessed. Where existing guidelines provided only indirect evidence, this was noted. Recommendations on healthcare policy, service provision, and mandatory reporting were based on best practices and human rights considerations. Relevant literature was systematically reviewed and summarized qualitatively, but GRADE was not used to assess the evidence for these recommendations. In cases where no evidence was identified, this was explicitly stated in the evidence summary.
